meta.purpose: Parameters for PersonalityVerse: infant temperament + life factors -> estimated adult Big Five baseline, probability of meaningful trait shift by a target age, and evidence-based change guidance.
meta.scale_convention: All effects are in population SD units (Cohen's d or z). To display on 0-100, use score = clamp(50 + 15*z, 1, 99). 'estimate': true marks values we derived or reconstructed rather than read directly from a source.
meta.honesty_note: Personality cannot be measured at birth. We model parent-recalled infant/toddler temperament as a weak predictor of adult traits (r ~ .1-.3), then add life-factor modifiers. Outputs are population-level probabilities, not diagnoses.

overall.solidity: Strong: meta-analysis, 62 effect sizes, >100k participants; robust to publication-bias correction.

per_trait_twin.solidity: Moderate: single classic twin study (123 MZ + 127 DZ pairs). Values sit above the meta-analytic .40 because twin designs inflate h2 vs family/adoption designs. Shared environment negligible for all five.

per_trait_recommended.reasoning: Shrinks JLV1996 per-trait values toward the VB2015 meta-analytic mean (.40) because VB2015 found personality model did not moderate h2 and single-study per-trait differences are noisy. Use for UI display.

shared_environment_c2.reasoning: Twin studies typically find c2 near zero for adult personality; Briley & Tucker-Drob fit AE models for this reason. Implication: parenting effects that are common to siblings are small; most environment is non-shared/idiosyncratic.

heritability_by_age.solidity: Strong: meta-analysis of longitudinal behaviour-genetic studies. Increasing stability with age is mostly environmental, not genetic.

rank_order_stability.description: Test-retest correlation r of a trait between age a (time 1) and a + lag years. Self-report, uncorrected for measurement error.

roberts_delvecchio_2000_bins.note: Population estimates by age at time 1, standardised to ~6.7-year retest interval in the headline values.
roberts_delvecchio_2000_bins.solidity: Strong and widely cited (152 longitudinal studies). Headline values from the abstract.

bleidorn_2022_models.solidity: Strong: largest meta-analysis to date (k=189 samples, N=178,503 for rank-order). Key update vs RD2000: little increase in stability after ~age 25.

recommended_function.true_score: rho_true = min(0.98, r_obs / 0.85)   # disattenuate for ~.85 short-term retest reliability of brief Big Five scales
recommended_function.reasoning: Age term = exponential fit to BL2022 points (reproduces .087@5, .567@15, .735@25, .819@50). Lag term = exponential fit to BL2022 lag decrements (k=0.119 reproduces .036@1y, .144@5y, .223@10y). The +0.082 re-centres the age curve to an assumed ~2.5-year typical interval, calibrated so the function reproduces RD2000 adult values (age 20, 6.7y lag -> .58 vs .54; age 50, 6.7y -> .73 vs .74). Childhood values come out lower than RD2000 (.07-.30), consistent with BL2022's finding of very low early-childhood stability.

very_long_term_check.solidity: Strong single study (Project Talent, N=1,795), useful as a sanity check for long horizons.

mean_level_change.description: Normative (average) change in d units per age period. N is the reverse of emotional stability, so N change = -ES change. Extraversion is split into social dominance (assertiveness) and social vitality (sociability); for a single E value use the mean of the two.
mean_level_change.per_year_interpolation: Within a period, spread d evenly across its years (e.g. C 22-30 = 0.25/8 = 0.031 per year).
mean_level_change.reasoning: Direction, timing and approximate cumulative totals follow RWV2006 (92 samples): social dominance, C and ES rise mostly 20-40; social vitality and O rise in adolescence and fall in old age; A rises mainly in later life; several traits change by ~1 SD cumulatively (RM2008). We could not retrieve RWV2006's Table 3 online during the hackathon, so per-period values are reconstructed to match the published pattern and cumulative figure. BL2022 broadly confirms: ES ~ +1.5 SD birth-80 (more than RWV), C ~ +1 SD then partial reversal after 70, A ~ +0.5 SD, O rises early then ~-0.5 SD across adulthood, E little change then slow decline. Verify against RWV2006 Table 3 before quoting exact per-period numbers publicly.
mean_level_change.solidity: Pattern: strong (replicated across meta-analyses). Exact per-period numbers: approximate.

clinical_and_nonclinical_meta.robustness: Only emotional stability survives small-study bias corrections in the controlled comparisons. O prepost not robust under PEESE (.04).
clinical_and_nonclinical_meta.solidity: Strong: large systematic review/meta-analysis, though most studies are clinical and pre-post; therapy type matters little.

HF2015.design: 2 studies, N=135 and N=151 undergraduates, 16 weeks, weekly self-report
HF2015.finding: Wanting to change a trait predicted change in the desired direction; implementation-intention coaching (if-then plans) boosted change; vague self-generated plans backfired.
HF2015.magnitude: Described as modest; per-trait d not reported in summaries.

H2019.design: N=377 students, 15 weeks, choose up to 4 weekly trait-relevant challenges from 50
H2019.finding: More completed challenges -> more desired trait change; accepting but failing challenges predicted change in the opposite direction.

modelled_d_per_15_weeks.reasoning: Hudson studies describe modest but significant change over ~4 months for engaged participants; we set ~0.2 SD for high engagement, scaled linearly by fraction of challenges completed, and -0.1 SD for those who sign up but complete <25% (backfire).

volitional_change_weekly_challenges.solidity: Moderate: correlational within-person designs, student samples, self-report only.

digital_coaching_app_PEACH.design: RCT, N=1,523 adults, 3-month smartphone + chatbot coaching, waitlist control, 3-month follow-up
digital_coaching_app_PEACH.persistence: Self-reported changes maintained at 3 months post-intervention.

per_trait_mapping.reasoning: Paper's headline effects are pooled across chosen traits; most decrease goals were for neuroticism. Use pooled values per trait; observer effects (~.35) are a more conservative 'real-world' estimate.

digital_coaching_app_PEACH.solidity: Strong for a single RCT (large, pre-registered, observer reports), but self-selected motivated sample.

guidance_defaults.reasoning: Blend of R2017 controlled per-trait effects, S2021 observer-rated effects (.35) and Hudson modest volitional effects. Conservative because users are self-directed without a coach/therapist.

temperament_to_trait.notes: Infant temperament is measurable from ~3-4 months via parent report/lab; effortful control only from ~age 2-3. Concurrent child temperament maps well onto Big Five (Surgency->E, Negative Affectivity->N, Effortful Control->C, Affiliativeness->A, Orienting/Perceptual sensitivity->O), but infancy-to-adulthood prediction is weak. App inputs are retrospective parent recall, which adds error; we attenuate weights by 0.7.

rothbart_factors.input_scale: Each temperament input as z (-2..+2) from 'much less than other babies' to 'much more'.
rothbart_factors.reasoning: Mapping direction from RAE2000 and ST2015. Magnitudes capped at ~.25 because (a) BL2022 rank-order stability from age ~3-5 over 20+ years is ~.1-.3, (b) Caspi 2003 age-3 group differences at age 26 were z ~ .1-.4, and (c) Chronis-Tuscano 2009 cites infancy-childhood stability .24-.64 only in extreme groups.

thomas_chess_types.reasoning: Prevalence from New York Longitudinal Study (textbook figures). Type-to-trait weights estimated by analogy to Caspi 2003 groups (well-adjusted ~ easy; undercontrolled ~ difficult; inhibited/reserved ~ slow-to-warm-up).

caspi_dunedin_age3_groups.description: Age-3 observer-rated behavioural styles (N=1,037; 96% retained at 26) and age-26 informant Big Five z-scores / MPQ z-scores.

undercontrolled.note: Impulsive, restless, labile at 3; highest negative emotionality (.27) and alienation (.34) at 26.

inhibited.note: Shy, fearful at 3; at 26 highest harm avoidance (.42) and constraint (.18), lowest social potency (-.31) and positive emotionality (-.29).

confident.note: Eager, quick to adjust at 3; highest social potency (.16) at 26.

reserved.note: Timid at 3; lower achievement (-.20) and positive emotionality at 26.

caspi_dunedin_age3_groups.solidity: Strong single cohort (Dunedin), effects small-to-moderate; age-3 style predicts adult traits after 23 years.

app_mapping.reasoning: Matches Caspi inhibited group (E z -.23) and Kagan's finding that most inhibited infants become less extreme.

kagan_behavioural_inhibition.solidity: Strong for continuity in extreme groups; weak for the population at large.

baseline_uncertainty.reasoning: With predictor-outcome r ~ .25, explained variance ~6%, residual SD = sqrt(1 - .0625) ~ .97. The app should show wide intervals around baseline estimates.

life_factors.note: Two kinds: 'baseline' factors shift the estimated current/adult level; 'event' factors shift expected change over the window in which they occur. Effects in SD units on each trait (positive = higher trait). N positive = more neurotic. Many associations are partly genetic or selection effects (people's traits also shape which events happen to them), so treat these as predictive, not causal.

factors.scale: for 'yes, significant' vs none; scale ~0.15 per ACE up to 4+
factors.solidity: N effect strong (meta-analysis 136 studies, N=526k, g=.46; mostly cross-sectional/retrospective). Other trait effects are estimates.

factors.reasoning: Small effects expected given c2 near 0 and genetic confounding; direction consistent with trauma literature (R2026) and twin findings (JLV1996, BTD2014).
Symmetric to harsh parenting but smaller; shared-environment variance is small.
Parental SES shows small correlations (r <~ .10) with offspring traits, largest for Openness.

Transition to university is accompanied by normative maturation (A, C, ES increase) and some event-specific effects; graduation is among strongest life events in BU2024. Most of this overlaps normative change, so use as an additive bump only versus 'no university'.

Social investment principle: earlier entry into adult work roles predicts faster maturation across 62 nations (B2013); first job among the largest event effects, work domain more consistent than love domain (BU2024).

Entering a first partnership in young adulthood predicted decreases in neuroticism and shyness and increases in extraversion, self-esteem and conscientiousness vs stable singles (eta2 ~ .04-.06 per trait); partly replicated 4 years later (C not replicated). We use about half the implied d (~.45) for regression/selection.
factors.solidity: Moderate: small German panel, replicated directionally.

factors.reasoning: BU2024 lists marriage among events with detectable but small effects; direction mixed across studies.
Divorce among stronger 'love domain' effects in BU2024; small.
Transition to parenthood showed little or no Big Five change vs non-parents, contrary to social investment predictions; minor self-esteem dips.

Over 1-4 years of unemployment, men showed growing declines in C, A (after initial rise) and O; women showed declines in A and non-linear C/O; re-employment within a year limited change. Magnitudes not in press summaries; set to small-moderate.
factors.solidity: Moderate study (German SOEP, N=6,769), magnitudes estimated; effects differ by sex.

factors.reasoning: Pre-post per-trait d from 207 intervention studies; mostly clinical samples, so for non-clinical users scale by ~0.6.
Negative life events predict increases in neuroticism, and neuroticism predicts more negative events (reciprocal); positive events predict small decreases.

meaningful_change.reasoning: Half an SD is a widely used benchmark for a minimal important difference (Norman et al. 2003) and corresponds to a 'medium' effect; it also roughly equals the cumulative normative change in C over a decade of young adulthood (RWV2006). For a strict individual-level test use the Reliable Change Index: |change| > 1.96 * SD * sqrt(2*(1 - reliability)), ~1.1 SD at reliability .85.

observed_rates.D2019_note: Project Talent age 16 -> 66; mostly in the 'maturity' direction (mean abs d ~ .63).
observed_rates.decade_reasoning: Derived from the probability model below (10-year r_obs .53 at 20, .63 at 30, .68 at 50; normative drift .1-.45 SD). Example: C from 30 to 40 gives ~34% up and ~17% down by >=0.5 SD; C from 20 to 30 gives ~43% up. These are true-score figures; with a strict RCI (~1.1 SD) the rates would be roughly a third as large. Treat as upper-ish estimates. Consistent with RM2008: individual differences in change are reliable and non-trivial at every age.

probability_model.formula: P(shift >= 0.5 SD in desired direction) = 1 - Phi((0.5 - mu) / sigma); P(any meaningful shift) = P(Delta > 0.5) + P(Delta < -0.5)
probability_model.mu: sum of normative mean_level_change over [current_age, target_age] + sum of applicable life_factor event effects (+ intervention effects if user commits)
probability_model.sigma: sqrt(2 * (1 - rho_true(current_age, target_age - current_age))), with rho_true from rank_order_stability.recommended_function
probability_model.reasoning: Treats standardised true scores at two ages as bivariate normal with correlation rho; individual change Delta ~ N(mu, 2(1-rho)). Standard psychometric construction; not taken from any single paper.

celebrities.disclaimer: Popular typing, not a clinical assessment. These are light-hearted estimates from public persona and common fan typings (e.g. crowd-sourced sites), not measured scores. Public personas are curated and can differ from private personality.
celebrities.scale: 0-100, 50 = population average. N = emotional reactivity/sensitivity (not a judgement).
